sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: This chapter presents the construction techniques and materials used for micropile installation. The construction of a micropile involves three primary operations: (1) drilling the borehole to the design depth, (2) placing the reinforcement (steel casing, reinforcing bar, or both), and (3) grouting the borehole. Each of these operations is described in detail, along with the equipment and materials used. The selection of specific drilling techniques, reinforcement, and grouting methods depends on the ground conditions, required micropile capacity, and site constraints such as access and headroom. Micropile construction is a specialty geotechnical construction operation that requires experienced contractors with knowledge of both drilling and grouting techniques.
key_points: Three primary construction operations: drilling, reinforcement placement, and grouting
Selection depends on ground conditions, required capacity, and site constraints
Micropile construction is a specialty geotechnical operation
Requires experienced contractors with drilling and grouting expertise
Site constraints include access restrictions and limited headroom

sections.title: Drilling Techniques
sections.body: Micropile drilling involves creating a borehole of the required diameter to the design depth. The drill hole may be created using a variety of techniques, broadly categorized as: (1) overburden drilling methods for advancement through soil, fill, and obstructions, and (2) open-hole drilling methods for advancement through rock. Seven overburden drilling methods are commonly used for micropile installation, as summarized in Table 4-1: (a) open hole rotary drilling with temporary casing, (b) rotary duplex drilling, (c) double rotary head, (d) casing advancement by crown drive, (e) casing advancement by Symmetrix or Odex systems, (f) hollow-stem augers, and (g) sonic drilling. The selection of drilling method depends on the soil type, presence of obstructions, required depth, casing requirements, and available equipment. Open-hole rotary drilling in rock uses tricone roller bits, drag bits, or down-the-hole hammers. In practice, most micropile drill rigs are truck-mounted, track-mounted, or skid-mounted rotary drill units with mast capacities suitable for low-headroom applications. Drill rig selection is often based on the most difficult ground condition anticipated along the length of the micropile.
key_points: Two broad categories: overburden drilling (soil) and open-hole drilling (rock)
Seven overburden drilling methods summarized in Table 4-1

Open-hole rock drilling uses tricone bits, drag bits, or down-the-hole hammers

Low-headroom configurations are available for restricted access sites

sections.title: Grouting Materials and Equipment
sections.body: The grout used in micropile construction is typically a neat cement grout composed of Portland cement and water. The water-to-cement ratio typically ranges from 0.40 to 0.50 by weight, resulting in a grout with unconfined compressive strength of approximately 28 to 35 MPa at 28 days. Additives such as bentonite (up to 2 percent by weight of cement), fluidifiers, and water-reducing admixtures may be used to improve grout properties. Sand-cement grout is not commonly used for micropiles because it is difficult to pump through the small-diameter tremie pipes and may result in incomplete filling of the annular space. Grouting equipment includes a high-shear colloidal mixer (preferred over paddle mixers for producing a well-mixed, lump-free grout), a holding/agitation tank, and a positive-displacement grout pump capable of delivering the required pressure and flow rate. For Type B pressure grouting, the pump must be capable of maintaining pressures of 0.5 to 1.0 MPa. For Type C and D grouting, higher pressures of 1.0 to 8.0 MPa are required. Quality control of grout includes monitoring the water-cement ratio, grout specific gravity (using a mud balance or baroid mud balance), and unconfined compressive strength testing of grout cubes.

sections.title: Grouting Methods (Types A, B, C, D)
sections.body: The four grouting methods correspond to the four micropile Types in the FHWA classification system. Type A (Gravity Grouting): Neat cement grout is placed into the drill hole by gravity head using a tremie pipe inserted to the bottom of the hole. The grout displaces any water or drilling fluid as the tremie pipe is gradually withdrawn. No additional pressure is applied. Type A grouting is used in rock and very stiff/hard cohesive soils where the borehole is stable. Type B (Pressure Grouting): Grout is injected through the casing or drill rod as the temporary casing is withdrawn. Grouting pressures of 0.5 to 1.0 MPa are typically maintained during casing extraction. The pressure forces grout into the surrounding ground, enhancing the grout-to-ground bond. Type B is the most common method in US practice and is effective in granular soils and soft to stiff cohesive soils. Type C (Primary and Secondary Grouting): A primary grout is placed by gravity (as in Type A), and before hardening, a secondary grout injection is made through a pre-installed grout tube at pressures typically exceeding 1.0 MPa. Type C grouting is predominantly used in French practice (IGU or IRS grouting). Type D (Multiple Repeat Injections): Similar to Type C, but uses a tube-a-manchette (TAM) or sleeve port pipe system to make multiple discrete injections of grout at specific intervals along the bond zone. Grouting pressures of 2 to 8 MPa are used to fracture the surrounding ground and grout body, creating an enlarged and irregular grout-ground interface. Type D achieves the highest grout-to-ground bond values.
key_points: Type A: Tremie gravity grout; used in rock and very stiff/hard soils; no added pressure
Type B: Pressure grouting at 0.5-1.0 MPa during casing withdrawal; most common US method
Type C: Primary gravity grout plus secondary pressure injection at >1.0 MPa; French practice (IGU/IRS)
Type D: Multiple repeat injections through tube-a-manchette at 2-8 MPa; highest bond values
Type B effective in granular soils and soft to stiff cohesive soils
Type D fractures surrounding ground creating enlarged grout-ground interface
Bond strength increases progressively from Type A through Type D

sections.title: Reinforcing Steel
sections.body: Micropile reinforcement consists of steel elements that provide the structural capacity to resist applied loads. The primary reinforcement types used in micropiles are: (1) steel casing (pipe), which provides both structural capacity and serves as a drilling tool in some methods; (2) reinforcing bars (rebar), which are continuous-thread, high-strength bars that can be coupled for long lengths; (3) hollow-core bars (self-drilling anchors), which serve as both the drill rod and permanent reinforcement; and (4) combinations of casing and center bar. Steel casing is available in various diameters and wall thicknesses, with yield strengths ranging from 242 MPa (Grade 40) to 552 MPa (Grade 80). Properties of common casing sizes are provided in Table 4-5. Continuous-thread reinforcing bars (threadbars, such as GEWI or Dywidag bars) are available in diameters from 26 mm (#8) to 63 mm (#20) with yield strengths of 517 MPa (Grade 75) or 1035 MPa (Grade 150). Properties are given in Tables 4-2 and 4-3. Hollow-core bars are available in outside diameters from 25 to 76 mm with yield strengths typically from 517 to 862 MPa, as listed in Table 4-4. The selection of reinforcement type depends on the design loads (compression, tension, lateral), required structural capacity, installation method, and corrosion protection requirements.
key_points: Four reinforcement types: steel casing, rebar (threadbars), hollow-core bars, and combinations
Steel casing: yield strengths 242-552 MPa (Grade 40 to 80); also serves as drilling tool
Threadbars (GEWI/Dywidag): 26-63 mm diameter; 517-1035 MPa yield strength
Hollow-core bars: 25-76 mm OD; self-drilling with drill bit at tip; 517-862 MPa yield
